title: Serving Runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking, and runbooks
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
-------
This document consolidates the serving runtime reference materials used by the eng-serving-runtime team: architecture overview, kernel scheduling policy, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for engineers who operate, optimize, and onboard new models to Redwood's inference runtime.

Goals and scope:
- Provide a single canonical reference for runtime architecture and policies.
- Describe deterministic profiling and benchmarking procedures used for performance claims.
- Capture operational runbooks and common troubleshooting flows.
- Surface known issues and mitigations so engineers can move fast with predictable outcomes.

Architecture overview
---------------------
Short summary: the serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference stack that routes requests, manages per-request KV cache, batches work, selects kernels and quantization paths, and streams responses to clients. Key design goals: predictable p95/p99 latency, high throughput per GPU, graceful fallbacks, and explainable performance trade-offs.

High-level components (service names used in logs and dashboards):
1) inference-router - HTTP/gRPC edge that authenticates, enforces quotas, and routes to appropriate backend (hosted/dedicated/private).
2) grpc-proxy - lightweight gRPC front for high-throughput routes (used by Dedicated).
3) request-batcher - continuous batching layer that groups in-flight tokens based on model, quantization profile, and latency budget.
4) kernel-selector - component that picks per-layer kernels (fused attention, flash-attention variants) and quantization execution (fp16, int8) based on model profile and hardware capabilities.
5) kv-cache - per-session prefix cache with LRU eviction and optional persisted cache for long-lived sessions.
6) model-worker (per-GPU) - executes batches using selected kernels and writes outputs to result-store.
7) metrics-exporter - pushes telemetry to Prometheus and traces to distributed tracing.

SLOs and perf targets (example profiles):
- Short-chat (seq_len <= 128, small prompt): p95 latency <= 120ms, p99 <= 300ms, throughput per A100-80GB: 150 prompt-requests/s (continuous batching enabled).
- Long-completion (seq_len 2k-8k): p95 latency <= 1.2s, p99 <= 2.5s.
- Embeddings: 5000 vectors/s per V100-equivalent (depends on embedding model).

Kernel scheduling policy
-----------------------
Objective: maximize GPU utilization and throughput while meeting latency SLOs. Kernel scheduling is enforced by the kernel-selector and the request-batcher. Policies are parameterized by: latency_budget_ms, batching_window_ms, model_profile (throughput/latency tradeoffs), and instance_tier (hosted/dedicated).

Policy rules (runtime-configurable):
1) Latency-first (default for low-latency routes): batching_window_ms = 8ms, max_batch_size = 64, prefer fused fast-kernels even if higher memory footprint.
2) Throughput-first (background or batch-only routes): batching_window_ms = 40ms, max_batch_size = 512, prefer memory-friendly int8 kernels.
3) Hybrid (for mid-tier): batching_window_ms = 16ms, adaptive kernel selection: start with fast kernel; if GPU memory pressure > 80% use memory-friendly kernel until pressure < 65%.

Kernel selection factors:
- model.arch (e.g., causal-transformer-v1, llama-family-3b/13b/70b)
- sequence length distribution (inferred from trace histograms)
- requested quantization profile (fp16, int8-symmetric, int8-ptq)
- hardware features: SM version, available shared memory, tensor-core availability, proprietary accelerators (if present)

Scheduling knobs and tuning guidance:
- batcher.max_batch_tokens: upper bound on tokens per GPU batch. Increasing improves throughput but raises p99. Tune by running controlled trace-based benchmarks.
- kernel-selector.memory_threshold_pct: triggers fallback to memory-friendly kernels. Set conservatively for multi-tenant GPUs.
- continuous_batching.window_ms: should reflect real SLOs; lower windows reduce p95 but reduce batching efficiency.

Profiling playbook (how to profile a regression)
------------------------------------------------
Purpose: consistent, reproducible steps to identify where time is spent (CPU scheduling, memcpy, kernel execution, serialization). Use this playbook when p95/p99 exceeds SLO or when change introduces unexpected tail latency.

1) Collect high-level metrics (start here)
- Dashboards: check per-model p50/p95/p99, GPU utilization, cuda_memory_used, queue_length, batch_size distribution.
- Alerts to consult: runtime-p99-latency, gpu-memory-pressure, request-drop-rate.

2) Reproduce with synthetic trace
- Use the local load-generator with a sample of the production prompt set. Command example:
  ./tools/loadgen --model llama-13b --profile ./profiles/llama-13b-chat.json --qps 50 --seq 256 --duration 300s --target-host <worker-host>
- Record the exact config (seed, prompt set, qps) and attach to the incident.

3) Collect system-level traces
- On the target GPU node run Nsight Systems for 60–120s: 
  sudo nsys profile --stats true -o /tmp/nsys_trace --sample=cpu --duration=120s --trace=cuda,osrt,opengl -- ./runtime-bench-wrapper.sh
- Collect nvidia-smi dmon concurrently: 
  nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 -o TD:csv -f /tmp/nvidia_dmon.csv
- Capture top/ps and iostat for the same window.

4) Collect kernel-level metrics
- Use Nsight Compute (or CUPTI-based metrics): 
  ncu --target-processes all --set full -o /tmp/ncu_report <pid>
- Metrics of interest: achieved_occupancy, dram_utilization, ipc, l2_hit_rate, tensor_core_utilization.

5) Per-request tracing
- Enable request tracing for affected model (trace-sampling 1%). Trace fields: request_id, batch_id, enqueue_ts, dequeue_ts, kernel_selection, kernel_exec_start, kernel_exec_end, memcpy_host_to_device, memcpy_device_to_host.
- Correlate traces with nsight traces to see where latency accumulates.

6) Hypothesis-driven remediation
- If memcpy dominates: enable pinned memory, reduce host-side serialization, and consider zero-copy paths.
- If kernel execution stalls on memory-bound ops: try alternate kernel (memory-friendly), reduce batch size, or apply a quantization profile.
- If GPU utilization is low and CPU queues high: move more of the pipeline onto worker threads, reduce serialization overhead, or increase prefetching.

7) Regression verification
- Re-run the synthetic trace and verify p95 and p99 improvement. Push a canary with a 1% routing rule and monitor for 24–48 hours.

Benchmarking suite (how we measure and publish perf)
---------------------------------------------------
The benchmarking suite is versioned and stored under tools/benchmarks in the monorepo. Benchmarks are deterministic workloads and include:
- microbench (single-layer kernel performance)
- modelbench (single-model throughputs and latencies for representative prompt sets)
- tracebench (replay of sampled production traces to validate end-to-end SLOs)

Benchmarking process summary:
1) Standardized hardware images (AMI/container tag) are used. Always record image tag, driver versions, CUDA, and cuDNN.
2) Run microbench to verify kernels produce expected FLOPS and memory bandwidth.
3) Run modelbench for each target model and quantization profile, capturing p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU util, and memory.
4) Publish results to perf-dashboard; results are annotated with git commit, container tag, and kernel selection config.

Benchmarking config example (table described in prose):
- config_name: llm-13b-fp16-low-latency
- hardware: A100-80GB, cuda-12.1, driver-535.XX
- runtime_flags: --continuous-batching=true --batching-window-ms=8 --max-batch-tokens=8192
- workload: chat-short-prompts (1k unique prompts mixed)
- targets: p95 <= 150ms, p99 <= 350ms, throughput >= 120 req/s

Release notes (recent highlights)
-------------------------------
- 2026-09-30: kernel-selector v2.3 deployed — added adaptive kernel fallbacks based on memory pressure. Typical throughput improvement: +12% for mixed-length workloads.
- 2026-06-20: continuous-batcher v1.8 — improved batching latency heuristics and enabled jitter-reduction which lowered p99 by ~18% for short chat.
- 2026-03-15: kv-cache persistence opt-in (experimental) — reduces cold-start latency for long-lived sessions; requires dedicated capacity or Private deployment.

Known issues and mitigations (short list)
---------------------------------------
1) Issue: p99 spike for long-sequence requests when batcher spikes to large token batches.
   - Symptoms: sudden increase in average batch token count, gpu-memory-pressure alerts.
   - Mitigation: enable hybrid policy or set max_batch_tokens lower on the route; enable memory_threshold_pct to 75%.
2) Issue: intermittent memcpy stalls on nodes with mixed CPU workloads.
   - Symptoms: Nsight trace shows long host-to-device memcpy times.
   - Mitigation: pin worker threads to dedicated cores, enable pinned host memory for the runtime, and isolate noisy CPU jobs.
3) Issue: int8 kernels produce rare correctness diffs on a legacy model variant under extreme sequence length.
   - Symptoms: eval regression with rouge/QA score drop ~0.2.
   - Mitigation: add regression guard in model-onboarding (disable int8 for that model until quantization tuning completes).

Operational runbooks (quick references)
--------------------------------------
Runbook 1 — High p99 on model X (triage)
1) Confirm alerts and collect timeframe.
2) Check batch_size distribution in the window.
3) Run synthetic load at 10% of production qps to reproduce.
4) Capture nsys trace and per-request traces.
5) Apply mitigation: temporarily lower batching_window_ms to 4ms for the route; if no improvement, roll back and switch to hybrid policy.
6) Postmortem: update model profile and add traffic-sampled benchmarks.

Runbook 2 — GPU memory pressure (> 85%)
1) Identify GPU and running worker processes.
2) Check per-model kv-cache and eviction policy.
3) If one tenant dominates, throttle that route (rate-limit) or move to dedicated pool.
4) If multi-tenant, reduce max_batch_tokens globally by 10% and rerun modelbench.
5) Schedule rolling node drain if memory fragmentation persists.

Runbook 3 — Kernel crash or illegal instruction
1) Collect core dump and container image tag.
2) Re-run failing request with debug kernel (debug flags enabled) in staging.
3) If kernel bug reproducible, revert kernel-selector config to previous known-good kernel and open a bug with kernel vendor/internal kernel team.

Team wiki and onboarding pointers
--------------------------------
- Start here: serving-runtime-team-wiki (internal index page) — contains links to kernel matrix, model profiles, and typical perf dashboards.
- Onboarding checklist for new joiners:
  1) Read runtime architecture and runbooks (this doc).
  2) Run localbench microbench on your laptop (or dev-gpu) to get familiar.
  3) Pair with an owner on a canary rollout.
  4) Review model-onboarding playbook for adding new models to the catalog.

Ownership and escalation
-----------------------
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime (pager: #oncall-serving-runtime).
- Secondary: eng-sre for capacity and infra escalations.
- Escalation matrix (short):
  - Step 1: oncall engineer (15 min)
  - Step 2: rotation lead (30 min)
  - Step 3: runtime tech lead + eng-sre (60 min)

Appendix: quick commands and snippets
------------------------------------
- Start local profiler: sudo nsys profile -o /tmp/trace -- ./deploy/runtime --config conf.yaml
- Dump batcher metrics: curl -s localhost:9180/metrics | grep batcher
- Query per-request traces: curl -s "http://trace-api.internal/requests?model=llama-13b&since=2026-11-01T00:00:00Z&limit=100"
